# The task

In single-probe change detection, participants see a set of items, for
example coloured squares, and after a short delay one probe appears at the
location of one of them. They answer whether the probe has the same feature as
the item shown there (the target) or a different one. Each trial yields one
binary response, and the probe can lie anywhere between the target itself and
the feature opposite it on the wheel.

`bmm` models the memory in this task with the same ideas it uses for
continuous reproduction, and adds a decision stage that turns memory into
"same" or "change". There are two such decision stages, and they lead to
different models of the same data:

- `tcc_cd()` compares a familiarity signal with a criterion
  [@Schurgin_2020; @Williams_2022].
- The `*_cd` models apply the Bayesian decision rule of @Lin_Oberauer_2022 to
  the retrieval densities of `sdm()`, `mixture2p()`, `mixture3p()` and
  `imm()`. These models are in development (GitHub issue #136) and not part of
  a release yet. This page describes them as they stand on the development
  branches and will change if they do.

This page sets out what each rule assumes, which data each model takes, and
how to compare them.

# A threshold on familiarity: `tcc_cd()`

The target confusability competition (TCC) model of @Schurgin_2020 treats
memory as familiarity. Remembering a target raises the familiarity of every
feature by an amount that falls off with the feature's psychophysical
similarity to the target: a feature `x` steps away from the target has mean
familiarity $d \cdot f(x)$ and Gaussian noise with unit variance. $d$ is the
memory strength, and $f$ is a similarity function measured in a separate
perceptual task, with $f(0) = 1$. In continuous report the observer picks the
most familiar feature on the wheel, which is the model `tcc()` fits.

With a single probe there is a single familiarity value, and the observer
compares it with a criterion, as in yes/no recognition. The probe looks
familiar enough when its signal exceeds the criterion, and the answer is then
"same":

$$P(\text{change} \mid x) = \Phi\big(\text{criterion} - d \, f(x)\big).$$

Schurgin et al. do not write this rule out. It is their familiarity model
with the decision stage of signal detection theory, which they name as its
origin. It is the likelihood of `sdt_yn()` with equal variance, one trial per
row, and a graded stimulus strength $f(x)$ in place of the 0/1 stimulus code.
A probe that matches the target is a signal trial and a probe with
$f(x) = 0$ is a noise trial. When every change is a change to the opposite
side of the wheel, as in the experiments of @Williams_2022, `tcc_cd()` and
`sdt_yn()` are the same model, and Williams et al. found that equal-variance
signal detection without guessing accounted for such data. Probes at
intermediate distances trace how the probability of "change" follows the
similarity function. The figure shows it for three memory strengths with the
criterion at the midpoint between 0 and $d$ (`bias = 0`).

```{r tcc-cd-curves, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Probability of a 'change' response under tcc_cd() as the probe moves away from the target, for an exponential stand-in for a colour similarity function."}
library(bmm)
f <- exp(-(0:180) / 20)
f <- (f - min(f)) / (1 - min(f))
deg <- 0:180
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 180), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Probe distance from the target (degrees)",
     ylab = "P(change)")
for (d in c(1, 2, 4)) {
  lines(deg, dtcc_cd(1, deg * pi / 180, d = d, similarity = f, bias = 0), lty = match(d, c(1, 2, 4)))
}
legend("bottomright", legend = paste("d =", c(1, 2, 4)), lty = 1:3, bty = "n")
```

What the rule assumes:

- Memory on a trial is one number per probe. Whether the target was stored
  well or poorly shows up only through $d$, which can vary between conditions
  and people but not between trials of one condition.
- The shape of the familiarity gradient is the perceptual similarity function,
  which you supply. It is not estimated, and a different $f$ gives a different
  $d$.
- There is no guessing state: a weak memory is a small $d$, and every probe's
  familiarity carries noise of the same size.
- The observer knows nothing about the quality of memory on a trial and uses
  one criterion for all trials that share a criterion term in the formula.

The data are the response, coded 0 = "same" and 1 = "change", and the probe's
distance from the target in radians. Set size and other conditions enter
through the formula, e.g. `bmf(d ~ 0 + set_size, criterion ~ 1)`.

# A Bayesian observer: the `*_cd` models

@Lin_Oberauer_2022 model the decision as a comparison of two hypotheses. The
observer retrieves a feature $x$ from memory for the probed location and
compares the probe $\varphi$ with it. The decision variable is the
log-likelihood ratio of the retrieved feature and the probe under a change and
under no change, and the answer is "change" when it exceeds a criterion. The
likelihoods come from the memory model itself: the memory model plays two
roles, once as memory and once as the observer's knowledge of that memory. In
`bmm` the memory models are those of continuous reproduction. `sdm_cd()`,
`mixture2p_cd()`, `mixture3p_cd()` and `imm_cd()` have the memory parameters
of `sdm()`, `mixture2p()`, `mixture3p()` and `imm()` under the same names,
plus `criterion`. The rule puts a "same" region around the probe, and the
probability of "same" is the retrieval probability inside it.

What the rule assumes:

- Memory on a trial is a retrieved feature, drawn from the retrieval density
  of a continuous-reproduction model, including its guessing or intrusion
  components where the model has them.
- The observer weighs the evidence with a model of their own memory. When
  precision varies across trials, the observer may know only how precise
  memory is on average (`knowledge = "limited"`, the default) or how precise
  it is on the current trial (`knowledge = "rich"`). Lin and Oberauer found
  that the decision model "works well in combination with all memory models
  when it is equipped with knowledge about constant characteristics of memory,
  but little or no knowledge about the state of memory representations in a
  particular trial" [@Lin_Oberauer_2022, pp. 43-44].
- The shape of the retrieval density is estimated from the change-detection
  data, through the memory model's parameters.

The data are the response, coded as for `tcc_cd()`, and the probe and target
features in radians as two columns. `mixture3p_cd()` and `imm_cd()` also take
the non-target features and the set size, as their continuous-reproduction
versions do.

# The two rules side by side

|                          | `tcc_cd()`                                              | `*_cd` models (in development)                                             |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Memory at test           | one familiarity value for the probe                     | a feature retrieved for the probed location                               |
| "Change" when            | the familiarity falls short of the criterion            | the log-likelihood ratio of change against same exceeds the criterion      |
| Memory parameters        | `d`; the similarity function is fixed input             | those of `sdm()`, `mixture2p()`, `mixture3p()` or `imm()`                  |
| Decision parameters      | `criterion` or `bias`                                   | `criterion`                                                                |
| Guessing                 | none                                                    | as in the memory model                                                     |
| Observer's knowledge     | none beyond the criterion                               | the memory model, on average or per trial (`knowledge`)                    |
| Data columns             | response, probe minus target                            | response, probe, target (and non-targets and set size for two models)      |

# Comparing the two rules

**On the same data.** Both kinds of model score each trial by the Bernoulli
probability of the observed response, so their pointwise log-likelihoods are
on one scale and `loo()` compares them directly. This differs from comparing
`tcc()` with `sdm()` in continuous report, where one model returns a
probability mass and the other a density. Fit both to the same rows, with
`distance = probe - target` as the column for `tcc_cd()`.

**The design decides what can be compared.** The two rules predict different
shapes for the probability of "change" as a function of the probe's distance
from the target. With only "same" probes and changes to the opposite side of
the wheel, each condition gives two response rates, which `tcc_cd()` matches
exactly with `d` and the criterion, and the comparison has nothing to work
with. Probes at several intermediate distances are what separates the rules.

**The similarity function is part of the TCC model.** `tcc_cd()` reads the
shape of the familiarity gradient from the similarity you pass, while the
`*_cd` models estimate the shape of memory from the data. A poorly measured
similarity function counts against `tcc_cd()` in any comparison, so use one
measured for the stimuli of the experiment.

**Across task formats.** Change detection and continuous reproduction can be
fitted with matching models: `tcc()` and `tcc_cd()` share `d`, and the
`*_cd` models share their memory parameters with the continuous-reproduction
models. Whether one person has the same values in both tasks is an empirical
question, and three things stand in the way of reading equal estimates as
equal memory:

- For TCC, the scale of `d` differs. `tcc()` fits the uncorrelated-noise
  model, which treats each option of the wheel as an independent signal.
  Schurgin et al. report that only the d' of their correlated-noise model is
  interchangeable with a d' from a same/different task, and that the
  uncorrelated d' is that value scaled by about 0.65 [@Schurgin_2020, Extended
  Data Fig. 2]. So on real data `tcc_cd()` should report the larger `d`.
- Continuous reproduction carries response noise that change detection does
  not have, which lowers the precision a continuous-reproduction model
  estimates.
- Participants encode differently depending on the test they expect. When
  delayed-estimation and change-detection trials were interleaved and the
  expected task was varied by its frequency, expecting delayed estimation made
  estimates more precise, while expecting change detection did not change
  change-detection accuracy [@CohenDallal_2023]. Comparisons between blocked
  tasks confound the test format with the way items were encoded; trials of
  both formats mixed within blocks avoid that.

A fit of both formats with shared parameters, which would test the
invariance directly, needs models for several responses in one fit. That is
planned for a later release.
